1:
Whether the mountains are mountains is the first question, and the answers run three ways. Wesley says flatly that they are the mountains properly so called, and Calvin refuses the alternative by name, holding that those who find judges figuratively pointed out here may be easily refuted. Gill reports the same figurative reading without dismissing it, that the chief men of the land may be meant, who stood as pillars to uphold the common people. Henry offers a third possibility and declines it: the address may be to the inhabitants of those hills, and some think the hills on which they worshipped idols are intended, but he judges it better taken generally, since the summons goes on to the foundations of the earth.

Why the elements should be summoned is where Calvin is fullest. His account is that the prophet had spent much labour on the people and derived no fruit, so he is at length bidden to call the mountains to bear their testimony, and the ungodliness of the people is proved before the elements themselves. There is an implied comparison in it, a reproach that ought to have touched them acutely: the mountains and the whole machinery of earth and heaven, destitute of reason as they are, had more understanding than these men. He adds a point of manner distinguishing this prophet from two others who did the same: they addressed the heavens and the earth abruptly, whereas this one prefaces his discourse by saying the summons was specially committed to him, so his hearers might know something unusual was coming.

The others reach the same effect by shorter roads. Ellicott calls it a solemn appeal to nature to hear the Lord pleading with his people, and points to the older song that opens by giving ear to heaven and earth. Keil and Delitzsch describe the chapter as a judicial contest between the Lord and his people: their ingratitude for great blessings held up, then the demand of righteousness and love and a humble walk in place of outward sacrifice, and last the punishment their violence and lying make necessary.

Henry finds two purposes in the command rather than one. It is meant first to excite the earnestness of the prophet, who must speak as vehemently as if he designed to make the hills hear him, proclaiming his message publicly as one neither ashamed nor afraid of it, and speaking from the heart because he desires to reach the heart. It is meant second to expose the people's stupidity: let the rocks and foundations of the earth, which have no ears, hear, since Israel, which has ears, will not. On the opening call he adds that what the prophet speaks he speaks in God's name, so they are bound to hear it not as the word of a dying man but of the living God, and that first or last he will be heard.

Clarke sets the chapter out as a dialogue with the parts assigned. God speaks the first five verses and convicts the people; the people, convinced of their iniquity, deprecate his judgments in the sixth and seventh; in the eighth God prescribes the way they are to be saved; and from the ninth to the end the prophet remonstrates at God's command. He calls the manner of raising attention awakening and sublime, since man is called to urge his plea in the face of all nature; and he explains why it was necessary, God having spoken to priests, princes and people and done everything needful to make them wise and happy, and been uniformly disobeyed. Their ingratitude, he says, is enough to make the mountains and the strong foundations of the earth hear and tremble and give judgment against them. Wesley agrees that the sin was so notorious that the whole creation might be summoned as a witness.
3:
That God should offer to answer a charge strikes Calvin and Clarke alike. Calvin says it seems unbecoming that God should stand ready like a guilty man to clear himself, and explains it as a concession, a personification ascribing to God a character not his own, since the prophet could not otherwise express that nothing blameable could be found in him. The address doubles their wickedness: God descends from his own elevation, speaks paternally, and takes the opposite side as though the question were to be discussed between friends, so the more kindly he deals the more their sin is enhanced. Clarke calls the condescension astonishing and puts it as a plea in court: they are called to show why sentence should not be pronounced, and if their answer is reasonable they shall be heard first. They are silent, and God states what he has done for them.

The two clauses of the question are glossed the same way by three. Wesley asks what injustice has been done and what burdensome impositions laid on them, and turns the second clause into a challenge to say what has made them weary of God; Clarke reads it as asking whether a fatiguing round of difficult duties had been required. Gill turns the address into the aggravation, that they were a people chosen above all others, redeemed from bondage and loaded with benefits, and sinned against him nonetheless.

On the deliverance the interest shifts to the three names. Clarke assigns each an office, the first as leader and lawgiver, the second as priest to transact spiritual matters in offerings and atonements, the third as endowed with prophecy to direct the women; supported from the Chaldee, which makes them three prophets sent to teach judgments, make atonement and instruct the women. Ellicott is interested in the pause rather than the persons: Israel, abashed, makes no answer, so the Lord continues to plead, the naming of the family to whom the decree was committed being his reply. Keil and Delitzsch put it plainly, that Israel cannot deny these gracious acts, and the memory of them recalls the ingratitude that repaid them.

Why the story of the hired soothsayer is singled out Calvin explains at length. The people in the desert were safe from Egypt, fed with manna and water from the rock, shaded by the cloud and lit by fire; yet the stream of mercy seemed stopped when a prophet came forth armed as with celestial weapons against them. Had God permitted the curse, they must have been stripped of every blessing; the cursing was miraculously turned into a blessing by a secret purpose. He could have recited every particular that proved their ingratitude, but thought it enough to touch on the redemption and mention this one kindness by the way. Ellicott makes it the strongest instance available: there is no more conclusive case extant of a man's will controlled to do the exact opposite of what he intended, the diviner being constrained to bless with every motive to curse.

The phrase naming two places divides them three ways. Clarke takes it of the interval in which the different answers were given, the camp advancing towards the part of the river opposite the second place, and reports the Chaldee reading, which makes it the wonders done between them. Ellicott would put a full stop after the diviner's answer and make what follows an independent instance, the incidents from one place to the other, explained from the sending of the spies and the passage after. Wesley reads it of neither, taking the first place for where the women of Midian were used to debauch Israel by that counsel, and the phrase for the length of the king's border along which it continued. On the last word Ellicott holds it means liberality or beneficence rather than righteousness, while Wesley makes it mercy, justice and veracity together.
6:
Who is speaking here is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Gill denies outright that these are the words of the people God had a controversy with, since what is proposed suits no such character even if the speakers were hypocrites, nor will he have them put into their mouths by the prophet: they are the Moabite king's questions to the diviner, asking what he must do to get the good will of a God who would let nothing be done against his word. Clarke has the people appear as defendants and, instead of disputing what is alleged, plead guilty at once and ask anxiously how the wrath of the Judge is to be appeased. Ellicott reports the first view, quoting a modern dean who writes of a short dialogue preserved not by the historian of the law but by this prophet, exhibiting the agony of the king and the lofty conceptions of the seer; then he sets it aside as less in harmony with the context than the conscience-stricken reply of the people, impersonated in some earnest speaker. Wesley reaches the same conclusion in a line, that a man whose heart was touched by the foregoing expostulation may be supposed to make the enquiry.

What the questions are for Calvin answers from the shape of the argument. He takes two things as granted: that the people are without excuse and forced to confess their sin, and that God had contended with them only to restore them to the right way. Had the purpose been merely to condemn them there would have been no need of such questions, for whenever God chides his people he opens to them the door of hope, provided those who have sinned repent. So the prophet asks, as with their mouth, what was to be done, glancing at the notion by which men commonly deceive themselves once proved guilty.

Henry follows the same movement but dwells on the enquirers. Judgment having been given against them and their guilt being too plain to deny and too great to excuse, they desire peace on any terms, and apply to the right person, the prophet by whose ministry they had been convinced; for who is fitter to show them the way than the man who made them sensible of having missed it. He notices that each speaks for himself, asking not what this man shall do but what he himself shall do, since every one knows the plague of his own heart.

The offers rise by steps, and Clarke grades them as they go. The burnt offerings are reasonable and according to the law, but insufficient. The thousands of rams might be procured, though with difficulty, and conscience answers that these will not do. The rivers of oil are absurd and impossible, and even if they could be got would make no atonement for such guilt. The last offer is not merely useless but sinful, though he notes that such sacrifices were made by two neighbouring peoples and the custom copied by the corrupt among Israel; and he takes the closing phrase as explaining the one before, whether the best of the children should be made a sin-offering. Gill keeps the whole within his own reading, taking the rams for what the Moabite king had himself offered.

Ellicott adds a note at the end, asking whether God will require the sacrifice of a possession as precious as the son was to the patriarch, and allows an allusion to real human sacrifices, either those offered by a king of Judah or the act of the Moabite king who offered his eldest son on the wall. Keil and Delitzsch state the function of the passage rather than its detail: the outward means of reconciliation are set up so that the next verse may overthrow them and recall the people to the moral demands of the law.
8:
Who is addressed here follows from what was decided about the two verses before. Gill, having made those the questions of a Moabite king, makes this the diviner's answer: not a reply to the body of the people, but to a single man who had consulted him and asked what he should do to please the Lord. Though a king, he was no more than a man, and the speaker would have him know it, especially in telling him his duty to God; and that duty, Gill says, the Lord had shown him by the light of nature, which is the work of the law written in the heart. Clarke takes the address as universal, reading the verse as the answer to the failed offers: every mode of expiation proposed is unavailing, since none can do away the evil or purify from the guilt, and God has himself shown what is good, what is profitable to the hearer and pleasing to himself.

Clarke then divides the three requirements and subdivides the first. To do justly is to give all their due, and he distinguishes three creditors: God, who is owed heart, body, soul and spirit, in the love that takes the whole strength; the neighbour, owed what one would wish done to oneself; and the man himself, whose soul must not be deprived of what God provided for it and whose body must be kept in temperance, avoiding excess in action and passion alike. To love mercy is to go beyond what justice requires into what kindness, benevolence and charity require. And the third clause tells how the other two are to be done: the Hebrew, he notes, implies humbling oneself in order to walk, acknowledging one's iniquity and submitting to be saved by free mercy, since no offering has availed; without that humiliation there never was and never can be any walking with God, for he must be a man's God before that man can walk with him.

Clarke does not leave the verse there, and his last note is the sharpest in the chapter. Many, he says, when they hear the nature of sin pointed out and the way of salvation made plain, shut their eyes to both and parry every exhortation with this very text, that God requires nothing of us but to do justly, love mercy and walk humbly with him. His answer is to put the question back, asking any such man whether he is willing to stand or fall by it.

Calvin comes at the same evasion from the other end. Hypocrites, he says, inquire how God is to be pacified as though very solicitous about their duty, and the whole enquiry is a disguise: by circuitous windings they turn aside and never wish to come directly to God. He observes that this is as common in his own day, the ungodly professing great concern, as though wholly intent on serving God, and yet seeking many bypaths so as not to be constrained to present themselves before him. The pretence is exposed by the fact that God has demonstrated in his law, enough and more than enough, what he approves and requires. Why then do they ask as though still uncertain? Because they are wilfully blind at midday: the law ought to have been a lamp to their steps, and they smother that light and do what they can to extinguish it.

Ellicott is the briefest and answers by two parallels rather than analysis. The first states the principle the verse turns on, that God sets more by mercy than by sacrifice. The second is the close of another book, where the conclusion of the whole matter is to fear God and keep his commandments, since this is the whole of man; which puts the three requirements here in the same class, the sum of what is asked rather than a reduction of it.
9:
Whether the voice cries to a city or cries to awaken is raised by two. Gill reports the second rendering alongside the first, and Calvin sets out the grammar: the word may be the ordinary noun for a city, or derived from another root and read as a verb, and if a letter concealed under the pointing is supplied the sense becomes to arouse. He prefers that as most suitable, since the people were torpid and as it were overpowered with sleep, and the voice of God ought to have been enough to rouse them. Keil and Delitzsch keep the city and identify it with the capital, refusing to take the opening words as a separate exclamation. Ellicott and Wesley agree on the city, Ellicott calling it the metropolis of the wealth and sinfulness of Judah, Wesley extending the address to every city while making the capitals principal.

Calvin uses the same verse to explain the prophet's own position. He complains that he and the other teachers did little, though their cry resounded and was heard by all; there was no excuse for ignorance, since God did not whisper in the ear of one or two but designed his voice to be heard from the least to the greatest. What he deplores is their perverseness, very few being attentive, so that the old proverb held and the song was sung to the deaf.

The clause about wisdom seeing the name is glossed by four in nearly the same terms. Ellicott takes seeing as regarding, suggests the sentence may be parenthetical like the warning that whoever reads should understand, and adds that such a man will perceive the hand of God in the visitations for sin. Henry makes it a definition: when the voice of God cries to us we may by it see his name, and it is a point of true wisdom to discover the name of God in his voice and learn what he is from what he says, though many are not aware of it because they do not regard it. He adds why the crying comes first: God warns before he wounds, being unwilling that any should perish.

Clarke alone maps the sins that follow onto the three requirements. The treasures of wickedness and the false balances show that they were not doing justly, since they did not give each his due; that the rich men were full of violence shows they did not love mercy; and that the inhabitants spoke lies shows they had not humbled themselves to walk with God. Ellicott renders the phrase the hateful ephah of leanness, and observes that this people were much addicted to falsifying weights; on the balances he would read not that God will count them pure but that he asks whether he himself can be innocent with such scales, quoting the law's stringent enactments, both the requirement of just weights and the prohibition of divers weights in the house.

The others fill in the parties and the goods. Gill takes the treasures for wealth collected unlawfully and kept in the house instead of restored to those defrauded, and reports two further renderings, one asking whether there is fire in the house of the wicked and another whether there is yet an honourable man persisting in his iniquity. Keil and Delitzsch put the emphasis on the little word yet, which stands before the interrogative particle for that reason, and Wesley gives it its force, that this continued after so many laws and examples of punishment. On the rich men Gill notes that they had enough of the world and no temptation to do an ill thing for money, and yet their treasuries were full of goods got by oppressing the poor; Ellicott says the same in a sentence, that the fraud was practised by men who had not even the pitiable excuse of poverty.
13:
Who is made sick by the smiting is not agreed. Gill and Wesley keep the received sense and apply it to the people, Gill taking the judgments of famine, pestilence and war to waste the state as a diseased body, Wesley saying the strokes will reach the heart until Israel is heartsick of its wounds. Keil and Delitzsch render it that God has smitten them with an incurable sickness. Clarke proposes something different: perhaps better, he says, that God himself is weary with smiting, having corrected them to no purpose, since they had stroke upon stroke and were not amended.

The rare word in the next verse produces three answers. Ellicott notes that it occurs nowhere else, derives it from an unused root meaning to be void, and offers hunger as a translation. Clarke reports a bishop's emendation transposing two letters to read that it shall be dark, which he thinks probably the true reading, the Arabic and the Greek appearing to have read the same, so the sense becomes calamity seated in the midst of them. Wesley keeps the received text and turns it inward, that they shall be cast down at home and by their own hands. On the clause about taking hold, Ellicott has them collecting their property for flight and failing; Wesley extends it to persons as well as goods, so that wherever they lodge their children or lay up their wealth the enemy will follow, and flight abroad will be no refuge.

Where the threatened losses come from Calvin alone explains. The prophet took his words from the lawgiver, it being usual with the prophets, when they wished greater authority, to quote the curses of the law literally; and God had denounced exactly this, that when they sowed their fields another should reap and when they cultivated their vineyards others should be the vintagers. The meaning is that whatever fruit the land produced would come into the hands of enemies, all being exposed to plunder; and he adds what makes it grievous, that men see consumed not only their provisions but the fruit of their own labour. Clarke states the same effect without the source, that they shall labour to amass property and not have the blessing, and whatever they collect their enemies shall carry away.

Ellicott turns aside at the olives to explain why the loss matters. The treading is of olives as wheat is trodden on the threshing floor, oil being indispensable for personal comfort; he supports its standing from the old parable of the trees taking counsel about a king, in which the olive was reckoned first, before even the vine and the fig.

The two kings named at the close are identified the same way and used differently. Gill traces the first from captain of the army to the throne, has him build the capital and set up an idolatrous worship established by laws and edicts, and makes the aggravation lie in the distance of time, those statutes being still kept many years after; he refuses the excuse that royal authority required it, since the command of God stood against it. Clarke calls that king one of the worst they ever had and his son a follower, describes their statutes as the grossest idolatry, and adds that the son's wife had no fellow on earth, a woman he thinks the model for a famous character of the stage, mixed of tigress and fiend; he renders the last word not hissing but a shriek, since those who saw them would be astonished and affrighted. Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch keep to the sentence, Wesley noting that the reproach is the one named in the law for a people who forsake God. Clarke closes with a judgment on the chapter, that few in the prophets or anywhere are superior to it for genuine worth, its structure being as elegant as it is impressive.
